# Flexible Intelligent Metasurfaces for High-Mobility ISAC: Hardware Evidence, Adaptation Timescales, and Validation Gaps

**Draft v0.28a — structured critical review — 22 August 2026.**

---

## Abstract

A flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) treats the physical shape of an aperture as a control variable alongside its electromagnetic state. Some recent system studies place that variable inside high-mobility integrated sensing and communication, where the delay–Doppler channel varies rapidly, and argue that shape adaptation follows it. Whether existing hardware supports that argument is this review's question: which operations in a FIM-assisted high-mobility link plausibly require fast adaptation, which may run on slower geometric or statistical timescales, and what has been measured about either?

We separate the architecture classes the FIM evidence base draws on, decompose FIM adaptation into ten stages from sensing to stabilised radiation, and record every timing value with its timed object, start and end events, and measurement status. Three results follow. No reviewed platform measures the duration of more than four of the ten stages, and the platform reaching four has no radio-frequency layer; the two best-covered platforms are disjoint at the boundary that matters, one commanding shape without radiating, the other radiating without commanding shape. No independently measured settling or post-deformation calibration duration is reported in the reviewed set, and stabilised radiation is timed only with geometry held static. Tracing the hardware-feasibility premises of the FIM system literature to their primary sources shows element-level response times presented as surface morphing periods, and a tabulated value with no counterpart in the cited source.

The contribution is the audit and the reporting discipline it motivates; we propose no hardware and do not claim the architecture is infeasible.

**Index terms** — Flexible intelligent metasurface, reconfigurable intelligent surface, integrated sensing and communication, high mobility, adaptation latency, hardware validation, evidence synthesis, conformal metasurface.

---

## 1. Introduction

A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) changes how it scatters by changing the electromagnetic state of its meta-atoms. A flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM) changes how it scatters by changing where its elements are. In the system-level formulation, each radiating element carries a coordinate along the surface normal; the vector of those coordinates defines the surface shape; the shape enters the array response through the propagation phase; and it is then optimised jointly with beamforming or sensing objectives, subject to a morphing range [1, Eqs. (1a)–(3), p. 13321; 2, Eq. (1)]. Simulated gains are reported across several formulations: a transmit-power reduction of about 3 dB at a one-wavelength morphing range for a multiuser downlink [2], further gains from introducing and then optimising a surface in a doubly dispersive multiple-input multiple-output ISAC setting [1, p. 13328], and element movement reported as more effective than passive phase control at enhancing received signal strength in a single-input single-output multipath scenario, with joint optimisation better still [3, p. 6823].

What distinguishes geometry control from electronic state control is that exercising it requires moving matter. An electromagnetic state change propagates at the speed of a tuning mechanism; a geometry change propagates at the speed of an actuator, a structure and its damping. The system models do not represent that difference, and are not obliged to: in all four FIM system papers reviewed here the shape is a variable that may be set, and the mechanism that sets it lies outside the model.

In quasi-static conditions, idealising the actuation may be less consequential for system-level performance. Under high mobility its timing assumptions become potentially load-bearing, because the state the surface was configured for goes on changing while the surface responds. At the operating point of the high-mobility FIM–ISAC study reviewed here, 28 GHz and a maximum velocity of 208 m/s, the maximum Doppler shift is approximately 19.4 kHz.¹ It is the combination of a millimetre-wave carrier with a velocity of that order that places the system outside the conditions under which the reviewed flexible and reconfigurable-surface hardware has been characterised: those demonstrations span a wide range of carriers, but none is characterised under mobility of this kind.

Three quantities must be kept apart here, and they are easily conflated. A Doppler frequency follows from carrier and velocity, and 19.4 kHz is exact given the stated parameters. A coherence interval is a threshold-dependent correlation statistic whose threshold is a choice, and the consequence of that choice is measurable: in a RIS-assisted high-mobility study at 2.6 GHz with a user moving at 90 mph, the interval over which the time-correlation function exceeds 0.5 covers 51 symbols, while the same paper's bit-error-rate comparison uses 20 symbol periods at 0.95 correlation and 40 at 0.82 [19, p. 721 and Fig. 4(b), p. 728]: one scenario, three answers spanning a factor of 2.5. An update deadline requires in addition a performance tolerance that somebody has selected, and this review defines none. What the Doppler figure establishes on its own is a regime, strongly time-selective, rather than an interval. The question that remains is therefore not whether the surface is fast enough, which cannot be answered without a deadline, but which operations in the loop are bound to the fast-varying state at all.

A natural next step is to ask how quickly a flexible metasurface reconfigures. The reviewed literature reports several such intervals, but they do not describe the same quantity. A scalable one-bit PIN-diode RIS reports an update time below 0.1 ms in its abstract and a tile reconfiguration below 10 ms in its results section [4]; both are correct, both bound the same 16 × 16 tile, and neither ends at a stated electromagnetic criterion, so the two orders of magnitude between them record a change of context rather than a change of speed. A liquid-crystal RIS reports approximately 15 ms and 72 ms, which are switch-on and switch-off transitions of a 4.6 μm material layer between 10 % and 90 % thresholds [5]. A flexible microwave metasurface reports 16.76 ms for an interval running from shape acquisition to bias-voltage supply, which contains neither the deformation that produced the shape nor any settling afterwards [6]. A soft shape-programmable surface reports approximately 30 ms for an isolated ribbon against approximately 300 ms for a full surface developing from flat [8]. These are not competing estimates of one quantity. They are measurements of different quantities, on different architectures, with different definitions of when the clock starts and stops, and quoting any one of them as *the* FIM response time yields a figure with no defined referent. Separating them, and asking what survives the separation, is the task this review undertakes.

Three broad reviews in the reviewed set border this territory and partition it cleanly enough to leave a specific hole. Saifullah *et al.* classify tunable metasurfaces by tuning mechanism and rank their speeds qualitatively, with electrical tuning preferred above kilohertz modulation rates, liquid crystal below about 1 kHz, microfluidic tuning on a millisecond scale, and mechanically stretchable substrates slow, environmentally sensitive and unable to address individual unit cells. There is no discussion of ISAC [9]. Tishchenko *et al.* survey multi-functional and hybrid RIS for ISAC, treat controller and network latency as a practical constraint, and link higher carrier frequencies to shorter coherence times, with no discussion of mechanical tuning [10]. Ma *et al.* survey reconfigurable and movable antennas and state the position closest to ours: mechanical movement is generally slower than electronic reconfiguration; instantaneous-CSI position optimisation suits quasi-static environments with long coherence times, while fast fading calls for statistical-CSI approaches that reduce movement frequency; and hierarchical cross-layer control, in which statistical information guides slow movement while rapid state changes are decoupled, is an open direction [11, pp. 3, 20, 26–27]. The same survey argues that future models should incorporate inertia, settling time, friction, backlash, movement accuracy and energy rather than idealised instantaneous positioning.

Two consequences follow, and the first constrains what this manuscript may claim. The slow-geometry, fast-electronics division of labour is established prior art rather than a novelty available to this review or to any FIM paper: statistical-CSI FIM optimisation has been published [12, 13], a two-rate schedule of element movement per subframe and phase adjustment per time slot is already embedded in a FIM channel-estimation protocol [3, p. 6829], and delay-aware modelling of reconfigurable apertures has begun in the adjacent fluid-antenna literature [14]. The second consequence is that none of the three reviews treats FIMs as a dedicated architecture under those terms: a full-text search of each returns no occurrence of "FIM" or "flexible intelligent metasurface", which establishes the absence of explicit treatment under that label rather than the absence of conceptually related coverage.² Ma *et al.* recommend that models include movement time, settling and energy; no reviewed source establishes which of those quantities have been measured, on what object, or under what definition.

That is the gap this review addresses, and the question it asks is:

> Which operations in a FIM-assisted high-mobility ISAC system must track fast channel variation, which may follow slower geometric or statistical change, and how well are the resulting timescales supported by existing hardware and control demonstrations?

We answer it as an evidence-mapping problem rather than a design problem, and within the literature reviewed here and the searches recorded in Section 2 the contributions are four.

**C1 — An architecture-aware, stage-resolved adaptation-chain framework.** FIM adaptation is decomposed into ten stages from sensing to stabilised radiation, and each source's treatment of each stage is coded on two axes: what the source establishes about the stage, and what it establishes about how long the stage takes. Applied to the reviewed set, no platform measures the duration of more than four of the ten stages, and the platform reaching four has no radio-frequency layer.

**C2 — A definition-preserving timing register.** Every reported value is recorded with its timed object, start event, end event and measurement status, and values may be compared only within a comparability class. Two common simplifications do not survive that discipline: an element-level update time cannot stand in for an aperture-level configuration time, as one panel's own two bounds show; and the reported ranges for electronic and mechanical processes overlap once the tuning mechanism is named, so an architecture label alone does not order them.

**C3 — A traceability audit of the hardware-feasibility premises in the FIM system literature.** Three premises are traced to the primary measurements behind them. Among the 13 of 20 candidate citing studies whose full texts were accessible, four reuse a timing value with its scope changed, and those four form one connected co-authorship network; the remainder cite the same hardware and attach no timing value at all. Every count is a lower bound on a partially observed set, and no prevalence claim is made. Section 5.2 gives the instances and the bounds.

**C4 — A statement of the validation gap and a reporting set that addresses it.** Four intervals are unmeasured in the reviewed set, and the reporting fields we propose prescribe definitions — object, start event, end event — rather than acceptance thresholds.

We propose no hardware, no algorithm and no control architecture. The manuscript is an audit, and it rests on the accuracy of its citations.

## 2. Review scope and method

This is a structured critical review. It is not a systematic review, a systematic mapping study or a scoping review, and it does not adopt PRISMA terminology, because it does not satisfy the requirement those labels carry: a reproducible, protocol-driven, multi-database *search*. What it does possess is a reproducible *extraction* protocol, and the two are distinguished here rather than blurred.

**Corpus.** The reviewed set comprises 24 distinct research contributions across 31 files. They are *distinct* rather than *independent*: several share authors, and duplicate versions, conference-and-journal pairs and same-group design lineages were collapsed into independence groups so that related publications are never counted as mutual confirmation of one another. Four of the files are supplementary-information or peer-review documents belonging to two of the papers; they are evidence *about* those papers rather than evidence alongside them. Three sources were readable only as page images, and no load-bearing claim is drawn from them.

The corpus was assembled by convenience rather than by a protocol-driven database query, so inclusion criteria are stated retrospectively and describe what the set *is* rather than a prospective filter: peer-reviewed articles, preprints and author manuscripts concerning FIM system modelling; flexible or conformal reflective and transmissive metasurface hardware; programmable mechanical surface actuation; electronically reconfigurable RIS hardware reporting timing or power; high-mobility channel estimation for reconfigurable surfaces; and reviews of any of these. Sources with no wireless, electromagnetic or mechanical-actuation content were excluded. Six sources were first read as preprints or author manuscripts; publisher-deposited records confirm versions of record for five, and the published full texts of the three carrying the most weight were obtained and inspected. Every load-bearing timing and parameter quantity keyed to them survives at the published locators, which this manuscript cites. One non-timing claim did not survive that check, and the affected statement is not used here (Supplementary Section S3).

**External searches.** Two searches supplement the corpus, and their evidential weight differs. A documented but non-systematic external search (ten queries, 17 August 2026) established whether a FIM-specific review exists, whether two-timescale or statistical-CSI FIM control is already published, whether any measured FIM actuation latency exists, and where the hardware-feasibility timing claims in the FIM system literature originate. It used a general web-search interface, which does not expose reproducible hit counts, so its results are recorded as search outcomes rather than as established absences.

A forward citation search (18 August 2026) is reproducible, and its two stages are reproducible in different senses. Stage one is automatic and deterministic for the dated search: every work citing the three primary hardware sources was retrieved through the OpenAlex citation graph, giving 306 records and 262 unique works after deduplication by identifier, of which 65 passed a title-and-abstract screen against an explicit wireless and communications expression. Stage two is manual and recorded rather than re-derived: excluding optics, photonics, materials, mechanics and imaging work, and collapsing versions under the independence rule below, leaves **20 distinct flexible-metasurface or reconfigurable-surface system studies**, of which 13 were read in full and 7 are behind publisher paywalls with no open deposit located. No access control was circumvented, and every count arising from this search is a lower bound. The seed identifiers, the query, the deduplication rule, the screening expression, the per-work decision table and the retrieved records as they stood on 18 August 2026 are available as runnable code and data in the accompanying public reproducibility repository;³ re-running the code against the preserved records reproduces the retrieval and this screen exactly, while a live re-query may return a different set, because OpenAlex is updated continuously. Supplementary Section S5 gives the full flow and the study-family register.

**Extraction.** Extraction, unlike search, followed a fixed protocol applied uniformly to every source. Each source is assigned to an architecture class with explicit transfer rules (Section 3); each source's treatment of each of the ten adaptation stages (Section 3) is coded; and every reported timing value is entered in a register carrying its timed object, a named start event, a named end event, a measured/simulated/projected/derived flag, the architecture on which it was obtained, and a comparability class. Two values may be compared only if their comparability classes intersect.

Four principles govern the coding, and each exists because a specific confusion is possible without it. The complete symbolic scheme, the seven-level evidence ladder used to grade evidence from analytical derivation through prototype measurement to end-to-end closed-loop validation, and the per-source coded matrix are in Supplementary Section S6.

1. **What a source establishes about a stage and what it establishes about the stage's duration are separate questions.** A measured radiation pattern is a quantitative result and not a timing; a fully delimited *simulated* runtime is a timing and not a measurement. Both are routine in this literature, and a single code would misread both.
2. **An accuracy is never timing evidence.** A root-mean-square deviation, a displacement error or any other accuracy figure remains an accuracy, however quantitative it is. We also distinguish a measured stage duration from duration information available only as a stated share, component or residual of a larger aggregate; from a rate; and from an interval the experimenter deliberately allocated. Only the first licenses the verb *times*.
3. **Evidence is never upgraded.** A system simulation is not hardware validation, a measured actuator is not a radiating system, an electronic switching time is not a mechanical settling time, and a protocol unit — a subframe, a time slot, an iteration count — is not a duration, since none of the sources reporting them supplies the numerology needed to convert.
4. **Independence is tested, not assumed.** A preprint and its version of record are two versions of one study; a conference paper and its journal extension are one lineage; supplementary material belongs to its parent paper; and independence between citing works is tested by author-set intersection rather than inferred from differing first authors.

**Absence claims.** Every statement about what is missing is reduced to one of two checkable forms: *this named document does not report quantity Q*, or *across the N sources in this named table, no row records Q*. No statement about the field as a whole is made anywhere in this manuscript. Absence of a measurement in the literature we read is not evidence that the measurement does not exist, still less that the capability is unattainable.

One further constraint is inherited by everything downstream. No reviewed source reports a repetition count or a dispersion figure for its headline response, morphing or adaptation interval, so none of the values on which this review's arguments turn carries an uncertainty. One subordinate process quantity does carry a dispersion — a function-evaluation cycle stated as 0.35 ± 0.15 s — so the deficiency is specific to the headline intervals rather than universal. It is a deficiency in the sources rather than in the extraction, and additional literature cannot retroactively supply uncertainty for values already published without it.

## 3. FIM architectures and adaptation timescales

### 3.1 Architecture classes, and what may transfer between them

Evidence about FIM feasibility is drawn from seven physically distinct kinds of system, and a statement true of one is routinely false of another. A response time measured on a filamentary mechanical mesh, an update rate measured on a rigid PIN-diode panel and a compensation loop measured on a bending varactor-loaded sheet are not three data points describing one technology; they describe three technologies whose measurements are nonetheless quoted in support of one architecture. The classes are therefore not seven things called flexible metasurfaces. Only A1 through A4 are named as flexible or morphing metasurfaces by the literature that uses them, and even there the naming is inconsistent; A5 to A7 appear because the FIM literature draws evidence from them, not because their authors claim the label. Distinguishing them is what allows the transfer rules at the end of this subsection to be stated.

Three questions distinguish the classes: what physically changes, whether the change is imposed from outside or commanded by the system, and whether the radio-frequency state is independently programmable. Table 1 answers them alongside the questions that decide what a measurement is worth.

**Table 1 — Architecture classes drawn on by the FIM evidence base.** A1–A4 are the direct classes; A5–A7 are comparator or evidence-donor classes whose authors do not generally use the FIM label.

| Class | What it is | What changes | Deformation source | RF state programmable | RF measured | Mobility evidence | Representative sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A1** | Theoretical FIM array with independently movable elements | element coordinates | an optimisation variable — no mechanism specified | in some formulations | ✗ — no hardware | simulated only | [1], [2], [3], [15] |
| **A2** | Flexible **passive** reflective metasurface | sheet curvature | external | ✗ | ✓ at fixed curvatures | ✗ | [16], [17] |
| **A3** | Externally deformed, shape-aware **programmable** reflective surface | curvature **and** meta-atom state | external | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | [6], [18] |
| **A4** | Actively self-morphing mechanical surface | commanded local displacement | **self-actuated** | **no RF layer at all** | ✗ | ✗ | [7], [8] |
| **A5** | Rigid electronically reconfigurable RIS | meta-atom state only | none | ✓ | ✓ | modelled / simulated only ([19]) | [4], [5], [19] (modelled) |
| **A6** | Movable / reconfigurable antenna system | position, orientation or internal state | self-actuated | ✓ (RA sub-class) | outside the reviewed measurement scope | — | [11] (review) |
| **A7** | Flexible **active** antenna array | sheet curvature | external | ✓ (per-element RFIC) | ✓ | ✗ | [20], [21] |

No source in the reviewed set demonstrates A1 hardware. The FIM system papers define the surface as a coordinate vector constrained to a morphing range and entering the array response through the propagation phase [1, Eqs. (1a)–(3), p. 13321]; they specify no actuator, no sheet mechanics, no inter-element mechanical coupling and no fabrication route. Where physical plausibility is argued, two mechanical platforms are cited: a liquid-metal microfluidic network in an elastomeric matrix, and an array of metallic filaments actuated by distributed Lorentz forces [1, p. 13320], citing [8] and [7] respectively. That is a plausibility argument and should be read as one. Both cited platforms are A4, and carry no meta-atoms, no bias network, no dielectric substrate and no radio-frequency ground plane. When a flexible reflective microwave surface was actually built, achieving mechanical flexibility required replacing a solid copper ground with a serpentine mesh, a change reported to reduce estimated bending stiffness by more than two orders of magnitude [6, p. 3].

The two realised surfaces in the reviewed set that are simultaneously flexible, reflective and electronically programmable are A3, and they share a property that the A1 formulation reverses. In the flexible microwave metasurface with shape-guided adaptive programming [6], a 480 × 240 mm sheet carrying 32 × 16 meta-atoms is bent by an external mechanical platform, a conformal array of 32 strain sensors reconstructs the resulting shape, and a trained neural network maps that shape to the column bias voltages that restore the intended electromagnetic behaviour. In the conformal reconfigurable reflectarray built from polydimethylsiloxane and printed liquid metal [18], a 10 × 10 array at 9 GHz with per-element PIN diodes achieves ±45° beam scanning using element-level conformal compensation phase, mounted on acrylic supports of different bending degrees, so each curvature is a separate static experiment and the surface neither senses nor commands its shape. In both cases geometry is a disturbance to be compensated. In the A1 formulation geometry is the *primary control variable* — the thing chosen to maximise an objective — and the channel is what is being tracked. Within the reviewed set, no source demonstrates that inversion in hardware.

The two A4 platforms supply every measured mechanical timescale in this review, and neither has an electromagnetic function. The filamentary mechanical metasurface [7] is a 4 × 4 mesh of thin metal and polyimide traces on an 18.0 mm sample, driven by distributed Lorentz forces, and uniquely in the reviewed set it closes a loop on shape, with in-situ stereo imaging feeding an experiment-driven inverse design. The soft shape-programmable surface [8] uses liquid-metal microfluidic ribbons in an elastomer, and can fix a programmed shape through a liquid-metal phase transition, a mechanism by which a slowly-set geometry could in principle be held without continuous actuation. These are the right platforms to cite for mechanical feasibility and the wrong platforms to cite for a FIM response time, a distinction Section 5 shows has not always been maintained.

Two adjacent bodies of work bound the problem from outside. A large conformal literature concerns apertures whose shape is known and does not change, and establishes that validated design methods and measured hardware exist for important fixed-curvature cases across several bands, phase resolutions and synthesis approaches — integral-equation synthesis accounting for finite size, coupling and spatial dispersion [22]; a reduced-order coupled-dipole model of a cylindrically conformal waveguide-fed metasurface [23]; an active conformal metasurface lens [24]; cylindrical RIS design carried from surface-impedance synthesis to a one-bit implementation [25]; a 3D-printed curved two-bit coding surface [26]; and a flexible liquid-metal-on-PDMS reflectarray holding its radiation characteristics across a ±25 % bending range at a fixed coding pattern [17]. That is prior art rather than closure, and it is prior art about a different problem: curvature is a design parameter there, not a control variable. Separately, flexible active antenna arrays (A7) supply the strongest evidence that large flexible coherent apertures are realisable, with two 256-element, 30 × 30 cm arrays remaining fully functional and programmable at concave and convex bend radii below 23 cm under closed-loop focusing driven by feedback from a remote receiver, and calibration explicitly targeting phase offsets caused by manufacturing variation, shape deformation and environmental change [20].

Four transfer rules follow, and are applied without exception in the remainder of the manuscript. A4 timing does not transfer to A1 or A3 without qualification, because A4 platforms have no radio-frequency layer and their measured response times bound a different mechanical object. An A5 electronic switching time is not a mechanical settling time. An A3 partial-loop latency is not a full-loop latency. And A7 is not A5: an active array's calibration architecture, which senses through its own transmit chain and closes a loop against a remote beacon, does not carry over to a passive reflective aperture, which has neither.

Figure 1 draws the consequence. Its two axes are properties of an experiment — has the platform demonstrated commanded physical geometry, and has radio-frequency performance been measured on it — so only platforms that performed an experiment are plotted; a modelling paper answers neither question, and placing simulation work in a hardware quadrant would be a category error. Three of the four cells are populated: the commanded-geometry-without-measured-RF cell by the two A4 mechanical platforms [7, 8], and the measured-RF-without-commanded-geometry cell by every A2, A3, A5 and A7 platform in the reviewed set [4, 5, 6, 16, 17, 18, 20, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. The cell requiring commanded geometry *and* measured radio-frequency performance together is empty. A1 does not occupy a cell in that map: it names the empty one, because the A1 system model is the specification of an operating point — geometry chosen by the optimiser, on an aperture whose radiation is what the optimisation is for — rather than physical evidence to be classified.

> **Figure 1.** *Architecture–evidence map of the reviewed hardware.* Both axes are properties of an experiment, so only platforms that performed one are plotted; the theoretical FIM performs none and is drawn as an annotation on the empty cell rather than as a platform. Within the reviewed set, commanded geometry and measured radio-frequency performance have not been demonstrated together. *(File: `figures/fig1_architecture_evidence_map.pdf`.)*

### 3.2 The adaptation chain

FIM adaptation names a sequence, not an event, and the sequence crosses three physical domains — perception, computation and mechanics — which have no reason to share a magnitude. Decomposing it is what makes it possible to say *which process a given number times*, and it is what turns an apparently contradictory set of reported latencies into a consistent picture.

| Stage | | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Sensing / acquisition | physical observation of the surface or environment — strain sensors, imaging, received pilots |
| S2 | Geometry estimation | conversion of raw sensor data into a surface-shape estimate |
| S3 | Channel estimation | acquisition of instantaneous or statistical channel state |
| S4 | Optimisation / inference | computation of the desired geometry and phase configuration |
| S5 | Control transmission | transport of the command from the compute element to the surface controller |
| S6 | Electronic state update | meta-atom electromagnetic state change |
| S7 | Mechanical morphing | the commanded physical displacement |
| S8 | Mechanical settling | decay of transient motion to within tolerance of the target shape |
| S9 | Calibration | re-establishment of the geometry-to-RF-response mapping after the shape changed |
| S10 | Stabilised RF operation | the interval over which the configured surface delivers its intended behaviour |

Across the four reviewed FIM system papers — three distinct studies, since one is a short version of another — stages S5 through S9 are absent from the model or assumed instantaneous. Geometry takes the value the optimiser assigns it, at the moment the optimiser assigns it. Section 4 records what has been measured for each stage, and Supplementary Section S6 gives the per-source coded matrix from which those counts are taken.

### 3.3 What the surface is being asked to track

Treating "the channel" as one clock obscures that a FIM-assisted ISAC system tracks several states with different rates and different consequences for failure: instantaneous complex fading, driven by Doppler; channel statistics and spatial correlation, deliberately treated as slower; angles of arrival and departure, which follow the user's traverse across the cell rather than the fading; target kinematics in the sensing subproblem; blockage, which is event-like rather than periodic; the geometry of the aperture itself; and the calibration state that determines when the aperture may be trusted again after a shape change. High-mobility models update angles explicitly and separately from fading correlation [19], and communication and sensing may impose different movement and update requirements [11, pp. 24–25]. The reviewed set fixes no relative rates among these states, and none of them carries an update deadline, because assigning one requires a performance tolerance the reviewed sources do not supply. Supplementary Table S7 records each state with its driver, the control variable it binds, and the evidence available for it.

The load-bearing question is which of these states drives the shape optimisation. It matters that the slow-geometry reading is not this review's reconstruction. The version of record of the high-mobility FIM–ISAC study states both halves of the trade-off explicitly: distributed Lorentz forces "enable rapid reconfiguration of the FIM surface shape within millisecond switching speeds", "comparable to typical channel coherence times in high-mobility wireless scenarios" [1, p. 13321]; and "the FIM surface shape can also be morphed once over several channel coherence intervals to achieve statistically optimal performance, thus offering a flexible trade-off between achievable performance gains and morphing speed requirements" [1, p. 13322]. The two halves pull in opposite directions and both should be taken at face value. The second establishes that operating the geometry on a slower schedule than the fading is a design option the system literature already permits, so the conditional framing this review adopts in Section 5 is a premise supplied by that literature rather than one imposed on it. The first is an assertion about another paper's hardware, and Section 5 traces it. A further FIM paper makes the fast reading more precise and equally untested: FIM surface shapes "are only updated on the timescale of the channel's coherence block" [29]. That is a legitimate modelling choice, and it asserts that command transport, actuation, settling and any recalibration all complete inside one coherence block.

Two costs are subtracted from whatever budget applies before any hardware acts. Pilot overhead scales with the controlled element count: the ON/OFF estimation protocol for a passive RIS requires 1 + M time slots to estimate the direct link and M reflected links sequentially [19, p. 720], while the FIM case acquires a two-dimensional measurement of Q subframes each containing T₂ time slots, with the element moving once per subframe and the phase adjusted once per time slot [3, p. 6829]. These are protocol units and we do not convert them to milliseconds, since the sources supply no numerology; but the overhead scales with the very quantity that makes a FIM attractive, and the FIM estimation protocol already contains a two-rate schedule, so the hierarchical structure a system architect might propose as a solution is present as a modelling premise before any hardware has been asked whether it can meet either rate. Computation is likewise not free. One reviewed FIM paper reports wall-clock computation time, and it is the only such measurement on a FIM-specific algorithm in the reviewed set: a clustering mean-field variational sparse Bayesian learning estimator on a stated desktop processor rises from roughly 4 ms for a small virtual array to roughly 100 ms at a virtual array size of 324, with the slowest benchmark reaching about 1.2 s [3, Fig. 8, p. 6833].⁴ It bounds nothing for an embedded implementation, but it *is* a measurement, which distinguishes it from the iteration counts the other FIM papers report in place of durations, and it scales with virtual array size: the computation that makes element movement useful becomes more expensive precisely as the movement becomes more ambitious.

## 4. Hardware evidence across the adaptation chain

This section reports what has been measured. It is organised by *what was timed* rather than by tuning technology, because one of the review's findings — that electronic and mechanical ranges overlap — becomes invisible the moment the two are separated into different sections. Before any value can be compared with another, the type of quantity has to be named: element switching, aperture configuration, mechanical element response, mechanical surface response, closed-loop convergence, open-loop replay rate and stabilised-radiation onset all recur here, and each is defined in Supplementary Table S2 with its start event, end event, timed object and the substitution it most often invites. Values may be compared only within a quantity type, and even then only when their objects and architectures match.

### 4.1 Flexible programmable reflective apertures

The flexible intelligent microwave metasurface with shape-guided adaptive programming [6] is the reviewed set's most instructive hardware source, and carries the most complete adaptation measurement available. The aperture is a 480 × 240 mm three-layer flexible sheet of metallic meta-atoms on polyimide, a polydimethylsiloxane substrate and a serpentine-mesh ground, with 32 × 16 meta-atoms at a 15 mm period and varactors driven over 0–30 V. Control granularity is columnar: the 32 columns share bias voltages, so the surface has 32 independently addressable channels rather than 512 independent elements. Measured operation spans 3.0–3.4 GHz with up to approximately 270° of reflection-phase tuning across incidence angles from 0° to 45°, the normalised reflection amplitude staying above 0.4 across all bias and incidence combinations. We report that floor as the source reports it and do not convert it into a radiation or reflection efficiency, since the source does not define it as one and the conversion would need loss accounting the paper does not supply. Shape reconstruction from the 32 strain sensors is validated against a stereo reference at a root-mean-square deviation as low as 2.36 mm at a maximum displacement of 45 mm — an accuracy, not a timing.

Its timing decomposition is the only one of its kind in the reviewed set. Data preparation for the network inputs takes approximately 4 ms, about 2 ms of sensor reception at roughly 1200 Hz per channel plus about 2 ms of processing; inference across 32 channels takes approximately 2 ms; and the bias-voltage supply module responds in 5.25 ms. The components sum to 11.25 ms, a figure the paper's own timing figure annotates beside the measured total of 16.76 ms, the residual of approximately 5.5 ms arising from full-cycle control of all 32 channels over an RS-232 link at 115 200 bps [6, pp. 4–5; Supplementary Note 6]. The methods differ between components, which matters for how much weight each carries: the 4 ms and 2 ms figures are thread-timing averages taken inside the control program, while the 5.25 ms figure is an oscilloscope measurement of the supply module's output following a control signal. The supplement adds that deformation intervals must exceed 16.76 ms for voltage updates to remain synchronised, expressed as reliable operation at deformation frequencies up to 60 Hz, and projects without measuring that under 10 ms would be reachable with faster acquisition circuits and a different communication protocol.

Three properties of the 16.76 ms interval must travel with it whenever it is quoted, and they are the reason it recurs in this manuscript. It begins at shape *acquisition*, so it excludes the deformation that produced the shape. It ends at bias-voltage *supply*, so it excludes any mechanical settling and any interval before the far field is stable. And the deformation is externally imposed: the supplement describes the mechanical platform as a frame carrying two telescopic links and three movable fulcrums, adjusted by hand to set the curvature, with no actuation timing and no closed loop around the shape, so the system compensates for a shape it did not choose. The interval is therefore a compensation latency, and reading it as a FIM adaptation time would misattribute it by at least two stages at each end.

The same supplement reports a second, methodologically independent experiment which, uniquely in the reviewed set, terminates at electromagnetic output rather than at a control signal. A finger-triggered sensor replaces the strain input; a dual-channel oscilloscope records the trigger on one channel and, on the other, received beam power demodulated by a logarithmic detector calibrated over −10 to −60 dBm at 3.1 GHz. The measured delay from trigger to stabilised RF output is 16.7 ms [6, Supplementary Note 6]. This review therefore cannot and does not claim that radio-frequency stabilisation is never timed in this literature. What must travel with the figure is its condition: the geometry is static throughout, and the interval contains no shape change.

What the platform establishes at application level is substantial and should not be understated. Mounted on an aerofoil model — the motivating scenario being aerofoil flutter under inertial, aerodynamic and elastic forces — it maintains a real-time QPSK video link at 3.1 GHz to a receiver 2 m away at 0° or 30°, with error vector magnitude staying around −20 dB while the surface is bent dynamically, and that demonstration is untimed. A second, independent flexible reconfigurable aperture confirms that such apertures are buildable: the conformal reconfigurable reflectarray of polydimethylsiloxane and printed liquid metal reaches 16.13 dBi peak gain with ±45° scanning at 9 GHz [18]. Its curvature is known a priori, it has no shape sensing, and it reports no timing of any kind.

### 4.2 Rigid electronically reconfigurable surfaces: the timing comparators

The scalable integrated RIS [4] is a one-bit PIN-diode surface at 9–10 GHz with 180° ± 20° phase difference, built as 16 × 16 tiles each carrying an Artix-7 FPGA, four tiles forming a 32 × 32 prototype. It reports an update time below 0.1 ms and a tile ON/OFF configuration update below 10 ms. Both are upper bounds rather than measured means, and — contrary to how the pair is easily read — both concern the same object. The abstract attaches the first to "each element", but no per-element measurement appears in the body: the figure traces to an end-to-end reconfiguration time for one 16 × 16 tile, about 40 μs over the Ethernet-based interfaces and up to 100 μs over USB/UART, against an internal FPGA update of about 40 ns once the configuration is stored [4, p. 6]. The second is the tile configuration update as operated in the near-field measurement campaign [4, pp. 8–9]. Both end at the configuration write, neither states an electromagnetic criterion, and as bounds they are mutually consistent. What separates them is the context in which each was stated, not the object or the technology — which is a direct demonstration that a reported latency without its start event, end event and object is not yet a comparable quantity. The same paper reports that the control network uses time-multiplexed latching, reducing the effective update rate to a quarter of the raw parallel speed, and reports what such a panel costs to run — 8.25 W with all diodes off, 13 W with all on, and 11.25–11.60 W during beam steering for the 32 × 32 array. Measured control power is rare in this literature and this is the only such figure in the reviewed set.

Those two bounds are *controller write* times in the sense of Supplementary Table S2: they run from a command issued by the compute element to the control state being written, and they say nothing about how long the tuning device itself takes to change state. The transition of the tuning material is a separate quantity type with its own start and end events, and the values reported for it in the reviewed set are numerically much larger without being measurements of the same thing. The liquid-crystal RIS based on defected delay lines [5] is the reviewed set's most carefully characterised material transition: a 4.6 μm liquid-crystal layer, 12 × 10 unit cells at 62 GHz, 6.8 GHz (10.9 %) bandwidth, insertion loss below 7 dB, and beam steering from −50° to +50°. Its measured response times are τ_on ≈ 15 ms and τ_off = 72 ms, defined between 10 % and 90 % thresholds and strongly asymmetric. A projection of below 2 ms for a 1 μm layer appears in the same discussion and is explicitly not a measurement of the fabricated device. Read as material transitions alone, the values reported in the reviewed set run from approximately 15 ms, measured on the fabricated device, to the tens of seconds the same paper attributes to reflectarray-type liquid-crystal implementations [5, p. 7]; both endpoints are liquid crystal. The semiconductor end of that quantity type carries no figure at all, because no reviewed source measures a diode or varactor transition: the flexible metasurface calls its varactor switching negligibly short and reports no measurement of it [6], and the mechanism survey ranks modulation rates rather than transition times [9]. Nothing here supports an inference that semiconductor transitions are slow, and nothing here places the sub-0.1 ms controller-write bound of [4] on the same scale as the 15 ms material transition of [5]. They are different quantity types, and on each of the two technologies only one of the two has been measured.

### 4.3 Commanded mechanical morphing, without a radio

The filamentary mechanical metasurface [7] achieves reversible out-of-plane deformation of about 30 % of an 18.0 mm sample using distributed Lorentz forces at currents below 27.5 mA in a 224 ± 16 mT field. Element response time is below 0.07 s, measured by monitoring a single serpentine beam with a 60 fps side camera and identifying the frame after which no displacement deviation is visible; system morphing is characterised as within 0.1 s. Its distinguishing feature is closed-loop control, with in-situ stereo imaging driving a gradient-based optimiser.

The cost of that loop is the most instructive number the platform reports, and it is fully visible only in the supplementary information. One function evaluation, comprising a voltage update, a wait for the sample to settle, a stereo capture with processing and a loss evaluation, costs 0.35 ± 0.15 s, of which 0.19 s is imaging and template matching and 0.1 s is a deliberate settling pause. Each optimiser iteration requires 4(N + M) + 2 function evaluations, which is 34 for a 4 × 4 sample, and convergence takes 5 to 15 iterations. The paper states the resulting figure directly: a 4 × 4 sample takes an average of approximately 2.5 minutes to morph into a shape from the zero-actuation initial state [7, Supplementary Note S6, Supplementary Table 1].

The separation between that figure and the platform's sub-0.1 s mechanics is exactly what the comparability classes exist to preserve, and it is large: the element response cited downstream as evidence of feasibility (below 0.07 s) and the demonstrated closed-loop convergence (approximately 150 s) differ by a factor of roughly two thousand, and the reviewed system literature quotes neither. What takes 2.5 minutes is *searching* for the voltages that produce a target shape on a nonlinear structure with a camera in the loop; once found, the same platform replays stored voltage sequences open-loop at a 10 fps update rate. Two things follow, and both are properties of this platform rather than laws. In the one demonstrated shape-control loop in the reviewed set, actuation is not the dominant contributor to loop time; sensing, perception and search are. Whether a radiating FIM would also be perception-limited depends on its sensing modality, its verification criterion and its compute load, none of which has been measured — but a closed-loop FIM's rate may be set by perception rather than by actuation, which is a reason to instrument the sensing path early, and no reviewed system model represents this stage at all. The same reported quantities also invite a substitution: multiplying the feedback-cycle time by the iteration count yields a convergence figure roughly two orders of magnitude below the value the source states directly, because an iteration here is 34 function evaluations rather than one cycle.

The soft shape-programmable surface [8] uses Lorentz-actuated liquid-metal microfluidic ribbons in an elastomer and reports a three-level decomposition that separates the quantities this review has to keep apart: an isolated ribbon responds in approximately 30 ms measured (approximately 50 ms by finite-element analysis); a full surface develops from flat in approximately 300 ms, of which approximately 250 ms is viscoelastic membrane relaxation; and shape-to-shape switching takes approximately 650 ms, being two surface developments plus approximately 50 ms of script processing. The element-to-surface penalty is a factor of ten, and the paper names its cause as the membrane rather than the actuator, which matters because a membrane is a materials property. The two mechanical platforms agree on the sign of that penalty and disagree on its size — a factor of about 1.4 for the filamentary mesh against about ten for the soft surface — and the disagreement is itself informative: the penalty depends on construction, and no reviewed measurement establishes it for a radio-frequency stack.

### 4.4 Flexible active arrays: demonstrated capability, no reported duration

The flexible active antenna array work [20] demonstrates two 256-element, 30 × 30 cm arrays at mass densities around 0.1 g cm⁻² that remain fully functional and programmable at concave and convex bend radii below 23 cm, and deliver approximately 80 mW of DC power wirelessly to a receiver about a metre away; the demonstrated steering and focusing ranges are stated by the authors to be limited by the measurement range rather than by the array. This is the closest any reviewed source comes to the operation a FIM would need after changing shape — re-establishing coherent aperture behaviour on a deformed, large, real radiating surface under closed-loop feedback — and it reports no duration for that operation. One qualification travels with it: this is an active transmitter with per-element RFICs, phase-locked loops and on-chip self-sensing receivers, not a passive reflector, and its calibration strategy depends on exactly that.
