The values in Table 2 measure different processes on different objects with different start events, and cannot be pooled. What they support is ordinal comparison within a quantity type, and Figure 2 displays them accordingly.

> **Figure 2.** *The timing landscape of the reviewed evidence.* Lanes are separate because the quantities are not commensurable: each was measured on a different object and architecture, between a different pair of start and end events. The axis shows where the reported values fall; it is not a latency budget, and no value may be pooled with, ranked against or substituted for a value in another lane. Two lanes carry no value at all — the mechanics of a radiating aperture, and its settling after a commanded morph. The two mechanical-loop lanes belong to the *same* platform and differ by more than three orders of magnitude, because one replays a known shape and the other searches for an unknown one. *(File: `figures/fig2_timing_landscape.pdf`.)*

Displayed on that axis, one observation about ranges follows, and it qualifies the standard dichotomy. Mechanical movement is generally slower than electronic reconfiguration, as the closest survey states qualitatively [11], and that is a reasonable first approximation which cannot be applied from an architecture label alone. An electronic material transition on one platform (72 ms) is numerically larger than a measured partial electronic chain on another (16.76 ms) and lies within a factor of about four of a full mechanical surface morph on a third (≈300 ms). Those three values were obtained at different frequencies, on different mechanisms, on different objects, with different start and end events, and they sit in three different quantity types; they may be displayed on a common axis to show that their reported ranges overlap, and they must not be treated as like-for-like performance measurements, pooled statistically, or used to infer the bottleneck of an integrated architecture. The qualification that survives is that architecture labels alone do not establish a universal latency ordering, so "fast electronics, slow mechanics" holds only with mechanism-, object- and architecture-specific qualification, and which stage binds must be established for the specific combination of material, actuator, control network and aperture in question.

### 4.6 Coverage of the chain, and where it stops

Three counts follow from the per-source coding in Supplementary Section S6, and they are not interchangeable, so each is stated with the axis it counts. Quantitatively evidenced stages: the maximum is six, reached by [6] and [7]. Measured stage durations: the maximum is four, reached by [7] alone. Stages carrying any duration information, whether measured or apportioned out of an aggregate: the maximum is six, reached by [6].

The platform that measures four stage durations is the filamentary mechanical metasurface [7], which times sensing, geometry estimation, control transmission and morphing, each with its own value and dispersion in its supplementary budget, and which has no radio-frequency layer at all. The flexible microwave metasurface [6] measures three — inference, electronic update, and stabilised radiation in the separate static-geometry experiment — and apportions three more out of its measured compensation-loop total, of which the control-transmission figure is a residual rather than a measurement. It does not command its geometry. Counted on the axis that permits comparison, the two sets overlap at sensing, geometry estimation, optimisation and control transmission, and differ exactly where the question lies: [6] carries the radio-frequency stages and cannot command a shape, while [7] carries the mechanical stages and does not radiate. Neither can be extended into the other by further measurement. Every other source is sparser still: one measured stage duration each for the liquid-crystal panel [5] and the soft shape-programmable surface [8]; none for the scalable integrated RIS [4], whose two reported bounds end at a configuration write rather than at a meta-atom state change and therefore bound an aggregate containing that stage rather than timing it; and none for the flexible active array [20], which demonstrates seven of the ten stages as working operations and attaches a duration to none of them.

Figure 3 shows the pattern by architecture class. Read across it, the stages sit on mutually incompatible platforms: measured morphing durations exist only on A4 platforms with no radio-frequency layer; no platform in the reviewed set measures a settling duration at all, the closest figures being a component identified within an aggregate on one A4 platform and a deliberately allocated wait on the other; electronic state transitions are timed only on A5 rigid panels and one A3 flexible aperture; sensing, inference and control transport on a flexible radiating surface are timed only on an A3 platform where geometry is a disturbance rather than a control variable; and post-deformation calibration on a deformable radiating aperture is demonstrated only on an A7 active transmitter, without a duration there or anywhere else in the reviewed set. Stabilised radiation is the clearest case for keeping the two axes apart: five platforms establish it quantitatively through patterns, gain, scan range, insertion loss or delivered power [6, 18, 5, 4, 20], and the one that attaches a duration to it holds its geometry static [6]. The gap is not that stabilised radiation is unevidenced; it is that its onset after a commanded shape change is unmeasured.

> **Figure 3.** *Adaptation-chain coverage by architecture class.* Rows are platform classes rather than individual papers; each cell records the strongest evidence any platform in that class provides for that stage. Fill colour gives the stage evidence status, and the appended marker gives the separate question of what is known about duration: **·T** a measured stage duration, **·(T)** a duration available only as a share, component or residual of an aggregate, **·[R]** a rate rather than a duration, and no marker untimed. The one cell that would carry an allocated interval — mechanical settling on the commanded-mechanical class — is marked † and carries no measured duration in either case. Several cells are quantitatively measured and carry no timing marker, because a radiation pattern, a gain figure or a delivered power is a measurement but not a timing. *(File: `figures/fig3_adaptation_chain.pdf`.)*

A total could in principle be assembled by taking each stage from wherever it was measured: the electronic loop from A3, plus surface morphing from A4, plus unmeasured settling and calibration terms. Such a sum would concatenate measurements taken on four different physical objects, one of which has no meta-atoms, another of which cannot bend, and none of which has both a controlled geometry and a measured radiation pattern. It would have the appearance of an engineering estimate while adding quantities that are not commensurable. What the decomposition licenses instead is weaker and far more defensible: within the reviewed set, no source times the adaptation chain end to end on any single object, and the reason is architectural rather than incidental.

Six capabilities nonetheless reach prototype-measurement level or higher: large flexible apertures that still radiate; in-situ shape sensing on three platforms; electronic phase reconfiguration timed at the controller; deformation-aware electronic compensation demonstrated over the air; commanded mechanical shape control with closed-loop verification; and conformal design at fixed curvature. None of these constituent capabilities is absent from the reviewed evidence base when considered separately, and separate demonstrations of them do not establish that they cease to constrain the design once combined, since integration changes the mass, the damping, the control granularity and the calibration burden of each. What no reviewed source measures is the intersection, which Section 5 states as the validation gap.

---

## 5. High-mobility feasibility and the validation gap

### 5.1 A stage-resolved answer

Assembling the demand side of Section 3 with the evidence of Section 4, the review question admits a stage-resolved answer rather than a verdict. Table 3 gives it, under one convention that matters: the "must it track fast fading?" column records a consequence of a stated assumption rather than a finding, and the assumption is named in the cell, because the central question of this review is which stages are exempt, and a table that presupposed its own answer would not be informative.

**Table 3 — Stage-by-stage answer to the review question.**

| Stage | Must it track fast fading? | Governing driver | Best available evidence | Evidence status | What this supports |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **S1** sensing (geometry) | no — tracks *deformation*, not fading | platform dynamics | ≈4 ms strain read [6]; 0.35 ± 0.15 s stereo cycle [7] | duration measured (A4); apportioned share only (A3) | geometry sensing at deformation rates; imaging, not actuation, sets the closed-loop rate on the one closed platform |
| **S1/S3** channel acquisition | **yes** | Doppler — ≈19.4 kHz at the reviewed operating point | 51-symbol >0.5-correlation window; 1 + M pilot slots | simulated / modelled — no measurement | the binding fast constraint, established by model rather than by measurement |
| **S2** geometry estimation | no | deformation rate | RMSD 2.36 mm at 45 mm against a stereo reference | **accuracy** measured (A3); processing duration reported only as a share of an aggregate | demonstrated |
| **S4** optimisation | depends on the variable | fading for phase; statistics for shape | ≈2 ms embedded inference [6]; 4–100 ms desktop estimation [3] | timing measured (A3); wall-clock on non-embedded hardware (A1) | a fixed pre-trained map runs in ≈2 ms; no embedded implementation of a *shape* optimiser is timed in the reviewed set |
| **S5** control transmission | with S6 | as S6 | ≈5.5 ms of a 16.76 ms loop over 32 RS-232 channels [6]; ×¼ multiplexing penalty [4] | residual share only (A3); the multiplexing penalty is a **rate**, not a duration (A5) | a major contributor at both measured scales; absent from the system models |
| **S6** electronic update | **yes**, if the phase layer is what tracks fading | fading | LC transition 15 ms on / 72 ms off, 10 %/90 % thresholds [5]; <0.1 ms and <10 ms tile configuration bounds [4] | **transition timed on liquid crystal only (A5)**; [4]'s bounds end at the configuration write, so they bound an aggregate containing this stage rather than timing it | a measured meta-atom transition exists for liquid crystal and is tens of milliseconds; the semiconductor control path is bounded below a tenth of a millisecond at tile scale, and **no semiconductor transition is timed in the reviewed set**. No deadline is defined here |
| **S7** mechanical morphing | **not necessarily** — no, *if* geometry is optimised from statistical or geometric state rather than instantaneous fading. That premise is assumed by the system literature and is not established (§5.2) | angular / statistical drift, *if* the premise holds | 30 ms element, ≈300 ms surface [8]; ≈2.5 min closed-loop convergence [7] | timing measured, **architecture mismatch** — no RF layer on either platform | mechanical timescales on non-radiating objects |
| **S8** mechanical settling | as S7 | as S7 | ≈250 ms membrane relaxation [8] | no duration measured anywhere in the reviewed set: ≈250 ms is a component identified within a 300 ms aggregate (A4), and the 0.1 s in [7]'s budget is an allocated pause | settling on a non-radiating object; no phase-relevant tolerance is stated by any source |
| **S9** calibration | no, but it bounds S10 | shape-change rate | closed-loop refocusing on a flexible active array [20] | capability demonstrated, timing absent | that the operation is possible on a deformed radiating aperture; nothing about its duration |
| **S10** stabilised RF | — | all of the above | 16.7 ms trigger → stabilised RF, static geometry [6]; EVM ≈ −20 dB under dynamic bending, untimed | measured for the electronic loop on a fixed-geometry flexible aperture; absent following a *commanded* morph | that RF stabilisation can be measured, and has been; no measurement of it after a commanded geometry change |

Three things follow from reading across the rows. The fast-timescale demand is established by modelling rather than by measurement: channel acquisition is the stage that must track fading, and the evidence for its timescale is simulated and analytical throughout, resting on a correlation window, a Doppler figure and a pilot-slot structure, and this review found no measurement of channel acquisition under high mobility with a reconfigurable surface in the loop. The electronic update stage has measured support only on liquid crystal, and no deadline against which to judge any of it; whether a sub-0.1 ms tile configuration bound is *sufficient* would require a stated update deadline for the same state variable, on a comparable architecture, at a specified carrier and mobility, against a stated correlation criterion, and none exists in the reviewed set. And the geometry stages are where the evidence changes character: morphing durations are measured only on platforms that do not radiate; no independently measured settling duration exists anywhere in the reviewed set; and calibration has been demonstrated on an object that does radiate, but was not timed.

Stated as an answer to the question posed in Section 1: conditionally on the two-timescale premise, that the shape is commanded from slower statistical or geometric information rather than from instantaneous small-scale fading, the fast, channel-dependent path comprises channel estimation, the optimisation that produces the fast state, the transport of that command to the surface, and the electronic state update; the geometry stages need not track instantaneous fading under that premise. The premise is stated as a premise. It is what the system literature assumes rather than establishes, and it is not this review's reconstruction, since the published version of the high-mobility FIM–ISAC study itself offers morphing once over several coherence intervals as an alternative to per-realisation morphing [1, p. 13322]. The support for the fast path is uneven in a way that is architectural: the requirement rests on analysis and simulation, while the hardware capability rests on measurements taken on rigid panels that cannot bend.

### 5.2 How timing values travel

The FIM system papers reviewed here do not claim to have measured their own hardware assumptions, and it would be unreasonable to expect them to. They do, however, rest on assertions about hardware that can be traced to a primary source, and the traceability matters because the substituted quantities are the ones Section 4 shows to be missing.

Two of the three premises are quickly stated. The first is that once surface shapes have been computed for a distinct channel realisation, "the optimized surface shapes can be used irrespective to changes in delays, Doppler shifts and waveform" [1, footnote 10, p. 13327]; traced to source, this is a footnote carrying no validity duration, no channel-statistics condition, no degradation bound, no sensitivity analysis and no experiment, and the paper's own simulations optimise per realisation rather than testing reuse. The second is that FIM surface shapes "are only updated on the timescale of the channel's coherence block" [29], which is cleaner and more testable, and which asserts that command transport, actuation, settling and any recalibration all complete inside one coherence block.

The third premise is the instructive one. A recent FIM system paper tabulates the "key parameters of existing FIMs", listing morphing periods of 30 ms for the liquid-metal platform, 10 ms for the filamentary platform, and 500 ms for a third, photomechanical platform not held in our corpus, and states in text that "the response time of FIM surface morphing reaches 10 ms according to Table I" [30]. Traced against the primary sources, the 30 ms entry corresponds to the liquid-metal platform's measured *isolated-ribbon* response, whereas that paper's measured full-surface development time from flat is approximately 300 ms and its shape-to-shape switching time approximately 650 ms [8, pp. 3–4]: an element-level figure has become a surface-level one. The 10 ms entry attributed to the filamentary platform does not correspond to any value in that paper's complete primary source package, which we obtained and examined in full: the main text, the Extended Data figures, the 71-page supplementary information and the peer-review file. The timing quantities reported there are an element response below 0.07 s, system morphing within 0.1 s, a function-evaluation cycle of 0.35 ± 0.15 s, and closed-loop convergence of approximately 2.5 minutes [7]. A full-text search of the package for "10 ms", "0.01 s", "sub-element", "filament", "transient" and "rise time" returns no occurrence, and the unit "ms" does not appear in the supplementary information at all. The tabulated deformation figures do trace correctly, since the 18 mm aperture and the ratio of about 0.3 match the reported sample size and 30 % out-of-plane deformation, so the entry is drawn from that paper; the year is additionally given as 2021 rather than 2022. One further observation bears on it: the element response was measured with a 60 fps side camera, a frame period of approximately 16.7 ms, so the instrument used to obtain the fastest mechanical quantity in the paper could not have resolved an interval of 10 ms. We record this as a discrepancy requiring verification rather than as an error, because no derivation or source for the value was found in any full text we inspected and the seven unread studies cannot be spoken for.

The resulting chain runs as follows. A mechanical-metasurface paper measures an element on a substrate with no radio; a system paper tabulates that value as a surface morphing period; a further system paper concludes that the morphing period is comparable to the channel coherence time and therefore that real-time adaptation is feasible; and the architecture is analysed on that basis. At no point in the chain is the substituted quantity measured on an object that radiates.

The reach of the practice was tested rather than assumed. Among the 13 of 20 candidate citing studies whose full texts were accessible, five instances of scope change occur, in four studies [1, 30, 31, 32]; the remaining nine cite the same primary hardware and attach no timing value at all, two of them sharing no author with either the network or the primary sources [12, 34], so restraint is the majority pattern within the studies we could read and is not confined to authors outside the network. The four studies carrying the five instances form one connected co-authorship network, which makes the independence result negative when measured rather than assumed: four different first authors are not four independent groups when common senior authors run through them. Two of the five instances were inserted between an author team's own conference or preprint version and its journal version, a pattern invisible to anyone reading only one version. Seven studies could not be read, and an abstract-level scan establishes nothing here because propagation occurs only in body text, so a further instance cannot be excluded. Every count is a lower bound on a partially observed set, and no proportion, rate or prevalence is estimated from it: this is a documented finding about one collaboration network, not a measurement of how a field reasons. The instance-by-instance inventory, the author-disjointness resolution for both the read and the unread studies, and the full study register are in Supplementary Sections S5 and S8.

Every one of those substitutions is enabled by the same thing: an informal term used where a definition is needed. "Response time", "morphing time", "morphing period" and "switching speed" all name a duration without naming the object it applies to, the event that starts it, or the criterion that ends it. The same failure mode can arise whenever an informal quantity name, an ambiguous unit and a plausible arithmetic step are combined, which is why it is better treated as structural than as a property of any particular author. The remedy follows directly: a timing value reported with its object, its start event and its end event cannot be silently rescoped, because the substitution becomes visible on the page. That is what Section 6 asks for.

### 5.3 What the gap is

The gap is narrower than a reader arriving from the system literature might expect, and misplacing it would misdirect the experimental effort that could close it. It is not a gap in any of the six capabilities listed at the end of Section 4, each of which reaches prototype measurement or higher and several of which reach over-the-air demonstration. It is the intersection, and it has a precise form: the transition from compensating a shape imposed from outside to commanding a shape and knowing when it has arrived, on an aperture that must simultaneously radiate. Within the reviewed set, every measurement of the commanded-shape side was taken on a platform with no meta-atoms, no bias network and no radio-frequency ground plane, and every measurement of the radiating side was taken on a platform where geometry is exogenous. That is the empty cell of Figure 1, restated as a measurement question.

**Table 4 — System assumptions, the hardware they imply, and the evidence available.** Evidence levels: L2 system simulation · L4 component measurement · L5 prototype RF measurement · L6 over-the-air demonstration · L7 end-to-end closed-loop validation with verified, timed stabilised radiation.

| System-model assumption | Where stated | Hardware capability implied | Closest evidence in the reviewed set | Level | What is missing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Element coordinates are freely selectable within a morphing range | [1, 2, 3, 15] | a radiating aperture whose geometry the system commands | commanded shape control on **non-radiating** mechanical platforms [7, 8]; radiating apertures with **externally imposed** geometry [6, 18] | L4 / L5, on disjoint platforms | **G1 — commanded actuation time for a radiating aperture** |
| Morphing is instantaneous, or completes within one coherence block | [1]; [29] | actuation plus settling inside a stated interval | ≈300 ms full-surface morph, ≈250 ms of it membrane relaxation, on a bare elastomer [8] | L4, **architecture mismatch** | **G2 — settling of a radiating aperture to an electromagnetically stated tolerance** |
| The optimised shape stays usable "irrespective to changes in delays, Doppler shifts and waveform" | [1, footnote 10] | a shape whose validity outlives the channel state it was computed for | no bound, condition, sensitivity study or experiment in the reviewed set | — | a validity duration, or an explicit statement that none is claimed |
| The geometry-to-response mapping is available whenever it is needed | implicit in all four | recalibration fast enough to be ignored | closed-loop refocusing of a deformed 256-element array, demonstrated but not timed [20] | L6, **timing absent** | **G3 — post-deformation calibration duration** |
| Radiation is trustworthy as soon as the shape is set | implicit in all four | a bounded interval from command to usable far field | 16.7 ms trigger → stabilised RF, geometry static throughout [6] | L5/L6, wrong start event | **G4 — stabilised radiation after a *commanded* geometry change** |
| Command transport and electronic update are free | all four; none states the assumption | distribution overhead negligible at aperture scale | ≈5.5 ms of a 16.76 ms loop is RS-232 transport [6]; ×¼ multiplexing penalty [4] | L5 — measured, and non-negligible | a model containing the cost at all |
| Geometry can be optimised against measured channel state | the premise of the whole A1 formulation | one platform holding aperture, shape sensing, channel estimation and optimisation together | four platforms, each holding **three of the four** | not attained | the integration itself |

The four unmeasured intervals deserve individual statement, because their experimental cost differs sharply.

**G1 — commanded actuation time for a radiating aperture.** How long from an actuation command to the intended displacement, on a surface carrying the layers a grounded reflective aperture is built from: meta-atom metallisation, a dielectric substrate and a ground plane. The stack differs for transmissive and active architectures, and the gap is stated here for the grounded reflective case the reviewed flexible platforms exemplify. The nearest available figures, tens of milliseconds at element level and hundreds at surface level, are for bare mechanical substrates, and the one flexible radiating surface in the reviewed set required a serpentine-mesh ground plane simply to permit bending at all [6], with its dynamic properties uncharacterised.

**G2 — mechanical settling to a phase-relevant tolerance.** No source in the reviewed set measures a settling duration in its own right. The closest figure attributes approximately 250 ms of a 300 ms surface response to viscoelastic membrane relaxation [8] — a component identified within an aggregate rather than measured separately, and it is a materials property of a bare elastomer. To indicate the form such a criterion would take, and not as a value this review recommends, at 28 GHz one wavelength is 10.7 mm, so a tolerance stated as a twentieth of a wavelength would be roughly half a millimetre. No reviewed source states a settling tolerance of any kind.

**G3 — post-deformation calibration duration.** The operation is demonstrated on a deformed 256-element flexible aperture using closed-loop focusing against a remote receiver [20], and no duration is reported. The alternative architecture, folding the geometry-to-bias mapping into a pre-trained network as the flexible microwave metasurface does, sidesteps the question by making calibration a training-time cost, but that approach is validated for a specific aperture, band and deformation family, and its generalisation cost is unmeasured.

**G4 — onset of trustworthy radiation after a commanded geometry change.** This gap must be stated more narrowly than the other three, because one reviewed source does terminate a measured interval at stabilised radiation. That measurement establishes both that the end event is well defined and that it is instrumentable with ordinary laboratory equipment; what it does not contain is a shape change.

Underneath the timing problem sits one that no amount of stopwatch work would solve. Within the reviewed set, no platform is architecturally positioned to optimise geometry against measured channel state. The flexible microwave metasurface has the aperture, the shape sensors, the inference engine and the controller, and no channel estimator; its loop closes on geometry [6]. The mechanical platforms have commanded shape control and closed-loop verification, and no radio [7, 8]. The flexible active array has the aperture, the sensing and the closed-loop calibration, and its loop closes on a beacon rather than on a communication channel [20]. Each of the four holds three of the four necessary components and none holds all four. That is not a measurement gap but an integration gap, and it explains why the timing gap has persisted: no platform in the reviewed evidence base is the object whose timing would need measuring.

> **Figure 4.** *System-model assumptions and the evidence link each one crosses.* Solid links are supported by a measurement on a comparable object; dashed links are not, either because the closest measurement was taken on an architecture that lacks a radio-frequency layer (red) or because the operation was demonstrated without timing, or timed from a start event other than a commanded shape change (amber). G1–G4 name the missing interval in each case. *(File: `figures/fig4_assumption_evidence_map.pdf`.)*

None of this shows that the missing intervals are large, or that the architecture is infeasible. It shows that within the reviewed set they have not been measured: these intervals are unquantified rather than quantified and found wanting. What the review does show is narrower, namely that in the specific feasibility claims examined here the confidence expressed exceeds the evidence traced behind it.

---

## 6. Implications and research priorities

### 6.1 A reporting set derived from the gaps

The deficiencies documented in Sections 4 and 5 are principally failures of *definition* rather than of measurement quality. Several of the values in Table 2 are excellent measurements; what they lack is the context that would allow them to be compared with anything, or that would allow a downstream reader to detect a change of scope. Once such a value enters a citation chain, an element-level figure can become a surface-level one with nothing on the page to signal it.

The set below therefore prescribes definitions rather than thresholds. We do not propose that actuation should complete within any particular time, that settling should meet any particular criterion value, or that any performance target should be met. The evidence supports no numerical acceptance threshold, and proposing one would introduce exactly the kind of unsupported figure this review documents. Each field is motivated by a recurring reporting deficiency or a specific unresolved quantity in the reviewed set, and those are different things: some fields name quantities no reviewed source reports at all, others name quantities that some sources report and others omit, which is what makes the reported ones incomparable.

**Table 5 — Minimum reporting fields for a deformable or reconfigurable aperture.** The ten fields whose absence caused the specific failures documented in this review. The full checklist, with the observed deficiency motivating every field, is Supplementary Table S4.

| # | Field | The failure it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Object timed** — one element, one tile, or the whole aperture | One mechanical platform's element and full-surface figures differ by a factor of ten; quoted without the object, either can stand for the other, and this review found an element figure tabulated downstream as a surface one |
| 2 | **Physical start event**, named | "Response time" denotes at least five different intervals in the reviewed set; one panel's two reported bounds, on the same object, differ by two orders of magnitude with no start event stated for either |
| 3 | **Physical end event**, named | Most reported intervals state no end criterion at all |
| 4 | **Threshold or criterion** defining that end event | The two sources that state one state incommensurable ones: 10 %/90 % amplitude thresholds, and the first video frame showing no visible deviation on a 60 fps camera |
| 5 | **Measured, simulated, projected or derived** | A projected sub-2 ms figure appears in the same discussion as measured 15 ms and 72 ms values |
| 6 | **Actuation and settling reported separately** | Bundled into a single "response time" wherever both are reported |
| 7 | **Deformation source: externally imposed or commanded** | The distinction between compensating a shape and commanding one is the central taxonomic finding here, and is rarely stated explicitly |
| 8 | **Whether a radio-frequency layer is present**, and what it consists of | Every measured mechanical timescale in the reviewed set was obtained on a platform without one |
| 9 | **Calibration procedure and its measured duration** | The one demonstrated post-deformation recalibration of a large flexible aperture reports no time |
| 10 | **Criterion for trustworthy RF operation, and the interval from command to meeting it** | Measured for static-geometry electronic compensation, so the end event is definable and instrumentable; unreported after a commanded geometry change |

Two further groups belong in any full report and are set out in the supplement: the mechanical fields — actuation mechanism and drive level, displacement in millimetres *and* in wavelengths, shape accuracy against the *commanded* shape, repeatability and cycles to a stated electromagnetic degradation, repetition count and dispersion for every reported interval, and actuation energy per shape change — and the control-chain fields, covering interface type and its measured transport contribution, serialisation or multiplexing penalty, computation platform and wall-clock inference time, and whether the loop is open or closed and on what quantity it closes.

The system literature cannot be expected to measure hardware. It can reasonably be expected to declare what it assumes, and the reviewed papers largely do not. Such a declaration should state which adaptation stages are assumed instantaneous — in all four reviewed FIM system papers, control transport, actuation, settling and calibration are assumed away and none says so; the assumed update rate for each control variable, and whether a two-rate schedule is chosen for tractability or justified by hardware; the assumed validity duration of a computed shape, with a bound, a condition, or an explicit acknowledgement that none is claimed; whether the cited hardware has a radio-frequency layer; and the provenance of any hardware figure imported into the paper, meaning what object it was measured on and what its start and end events were. The last item is the most consequential: a table of imported hardware parameters carrying an "object measured" column and a "start/end events" column would have made the traceability audit of §5.2 unnecessary, and the scope change documented there would have been explicit on the page.

We do not propose this as a standard. We propose it as the minimum set that would have allowed the questions in this review to be answered from the published record. Some of its fields could be reported from measurements already performed; others require new ones.

### 6.2 What follows for system modelling

Three consequences, in descending order of confidence. The first is to report the object: the most common failure observed here is not optimism but underspecification, and a latency without an object is uninterpretable. System papers importing hardware figures should import the object with them.

The second is not to assume the electronic layer is uniformly fast. Electronic update latency is mechanism-dependent: the reviewed liquid-crystal device exhibits tens-of-milliseconds transitions at the layer thickness measured, whereas semiconductor control reports different quantities at different granularities, neither of them a material transition time. Whether either mechanism satisfies a particular fast-loop requirement depends on the required state-validity interval and on the architecture, and no reviewed source establishes a scenario-specific deadline against which to judge.

The third is to model the control network. Aperture-scale command distribution can be a major contributor to update latency — a stated factor-of-four serialisation penalty on one measured panel, roughly a third of the measured loop on the other — and it is absent from the FIM system models reviewed here. We claim no dominance, since the two platforms do not agree closely enough to support one and neither reports the decomposition that would settle it; the implication survives either reading, because it concerns whether the cost is modelled at all rather than how large it is. The reviewed system papers simulate 4 to 16 movable elements while the measured hardware has 32, 256 or 512 controllable channels, so a cost that scales with channel count is invisible at the scale the theory currently explores, and the theory's element counts are more likely to grow than shrink as apertures scale.

### 6.3 The highest-value missing measurements

The gap is narrow enough to name three experiments. They are ordered below by how much new hardware each appears to require, which is a judgement about experimental prerequisites and not the result of a cost study; we have performed none.

**Time an experiment that already exists.** G3 appears to require the least new hardware, because the apparatus has already been assembled once: closed-loop recalibration of a deformed 256-element flexible active array is demonstrated but not timed. If that platform remains available, adding synchronised timing from the curvature change to the re-converged focus, at a stated performance tolerance, would convert the reviewed set's strongest qualitative demonstration into a quantitative constraint without a new aperture prototype. Whether the apparatus is still available, whether the deformation and the radio-frequency measurement can be triggered against a common clock, and how reproducible the interval proves to be are unknown to us.

**Instrument a flexible reflective aperture mechanically.** G1 and G2 could be investigated by integrating already-demonstrated classes of flexible radio-frequency apertures and actuation mechanisms in one instrumented experiment, measuring displacement, settling against a stated and justified electromagnetic criterion, and the resulting reflection-phase transient. We prescribe no particular fraction of a wavelength; choosing and justifying one is part of the experiment. Both the apertures and the actuation mechanisms exist separately; integrating actuation with a radiating flexible stack is itself an engineering problem, and within the reviewed set the combination has not been built and timed. It would also settle whether the element-level figures now in circulation bear any relation to a radiating aperture. G4 follows from these and requires a radio-frequency measurement synchronised to the actuation command, which is the natural output of the same experiment.

**Close a loop on a channel.** The integration gap is a research programme rather than an experiment. It requires a platform that senses geometry, estimates a channel, optimises both geometry and phase, actuates, and measures the resulting link. Nothing in the reviewed literature is close to it, and no timeline should be asserted for it.

### 6.4 Limitations

The search was not systematic. Sources were assembled by convenience and supplemented by a documented external search, with no protocol-driven indexed-database queries and no second screener. The forward citation search of §5.2 is the exception in being reproducible, and it too is bounded: 13 of the 20 relevant system studies were obtainable in full text and 7 are behind publisher paywalls, so the practice could extend into papers we could not read, and every count reported is a lower bound.

No reviewed source reports uncertainty on a headline timing value. Neither supplementary package states a repetition count, a sample size or a dispersion figure for its principal interval, although one subordinate quantity is stated as 0.35 ± 0.15 s, which shows the deficiency is real rather than assumed: those authors did report dispersion where they had it. The headline intervals are single stated figures.

Three sources were readable only as page images, their metadata and abstracts read from rendered pages, and no load-bearing claim is drawn from them. Some sources remain identified bibliographically only, and quantitative claims keyed to them should be re-verified against their published versions before submission.

Extraction and classification were performed by a single reviewer and were not independently duplicated or adjudicated. Architecture assignment, stage coding, the timing-status judgements and evidence-level assignment each rest on one reader's judgement, with no second screener and no disagreement-resolution procedure. The boundaries most exposed to this are "assumed" against "unclear", and the distinction between a timed interval and one marked as incompletely defined. A duplicated extraction is the single methodological improvement most likely to change a cell.

The reviewed set is small. Twenty-four distinct contributions is enough to support the specific traceability and definitional findings, and not enough to support any statistical statement about the literature; we make none.

---

## 7. Conclusion

This review asked which operations in a FIM-assisted high-mobility ISAC system must track fast channel variation, which may follow slower geometric or statistical change, and how well existing hardware supports the resulting timescales. The stage-resolved answer is that, conditionally on the two-timescale premise the system literature itself supplies, the fast path comprises channel estimation, the optimisation that produces the fast state, the transport of that command to the surface, and the electronic state update; the geometry stages of sensing, morphing, settling and geometry-dependent calibration need not track instantaneous fading under that premise. The evidence behind those two groups is asymmetric, and in the opposite direction to the usual presentation: the demand on the fast path is established by analysis and simulation, while the hardware capability on it is measured, and measured on rigid panels that cannot bend.

The central validation gap is the intersection rather than the ingredients. Large flexible apertures radiate and remain programmable while bent; surface shape can be sensed in situ; electronic state updates on a semiconductor panel have been timed at the controller; commanded mechanical shape control has been demonstrated with closed-loop verification. Each was demonstrated on a platform lacking one of the things a FIM needs together: a radiating layer, a geometry the system commands, and a channel it observes. Within the reviewed set, four platforms each hold three of the four necessary components and none holds all four, so no reviewed source times the adaptation chain end to end on one object, none measures the duration of more than four of the ten stages, and the platform reaching four does not radiate. Four intervals are unmeasured: commanded actuation of a radiating aperture, settling of one to an electromagnetically stated tolerance, post-deformation calibration duration, and the onset of trustworthy radiation after a commanded geometry change.

The contribution is the audit and the reporting discipline it motivates: a taxonomy stating which measurements may transfer between physically different platforms, a decomposition stating which process a number times, a register recording the definitions, a traceability result bounded to the cases in which it was verified, and a reporting set derived from the observed deficiencies. Three substitutions are unsafe, each demonstrated by a value in the register rather than asserted: an element-level figure is not an aperture-level one; a partial electronic compensation loop is not an adaptation latency; and an interval ending in stabilised radiation, measured with the geometry held static, is not a measurement of stabilisation after a commanded morph. We make no novelty claim for the two-timescale or statistical-CSI principle, which is established in the movable-antenna and FIM literatures, and we propose no new hardware or control algorithm.

Among the gaps identified, timing the recalibration experiment that has already been performed appears to require the least new hardware: post-deformation closed-loop recalibration of a large flexible aperture has been demonstrated and not timed. Synchronised timing from a curvature change to a re-converged focus, at a stated performance tolerance, would convert that demonstration into a quantitative constraint, provided the apparatus remains available and the two events can be timestamped against a common clock. Alongside it, reporting the object, the start event and the end event of every published interval would have prevented every substitution documented in §5.2.

Two limits bound all of this. The corpus was assembled by convenience rather than by protocol, so absence of a measurement in the literature we read is not evidence that the measurement does not exist, still less that the capability is unattainable; every absence stated here is bounded to the reviewed set or to the documented searches. The traceability finding is bounded twice over, by that set and by full-text access to 13 of the 20 candidate studies. Whether flexible intelligent metasurfaces work in high mobility remains open. The narrower claim made here is that in the cases traced, the confidence expressed in the feasibility premises exceeds the evidence traced behind them.
